vignette:
He is a 68-year-old school counselor, a man who has spent forty-two years guiding teenagers through their worst moments. He still wears the same style of corduroy blazer he wore in the 1980s, and his office has a plastic plant on the filing cabinet because the real one kept dying. He is married to a retired librarian, and they have two grown children who live three states away. He tells these facts the way someone recites lines they have memorized but no longer believe.

Three years ago, on a Tuesday evening in late October, he stopped at a gas station on his way home from a parent-teacher conference. A man asked him for money, and he reached for his wallet. The man hit him twice in the face with a tire iron. The first blow shattered his cheekbone. The second broke his jaw and knocked him unconscious. He woke up in the ER with his wife holding his hand, her face pale, her voice saying his name over and over as if she were calling him back from a great distance.

The physical recovery took months. But what returned, piece by piece, was not the same man. He began to notice things. He notices everything now. Every person who walks too close behind him. Every sudden movement in his peripheral vision. Every sound that is unexpected, every shadow that falls wrong. He scans parking lots before he gets out of his car. He sits with his back to the wall in restaurants, and when his wife asks him what he is looking at, he says, “Nothing,” and does not explain.

At work, he is still the same counselor on the surface. He listens to kids talk about their anxieties, their broken homes, their dread of the future. But now, when a boy raises his voice in the hallway, something cold blooms in his chest. When a student walks into his office angry and slams a book on his desk, he feels his heart surge and his breath go shallow. He has to excuse himself to the bathroom, where he stands with his hands on the sink and tells himself, You are safe. That is a child. You are safe. The words do not help, but he says them anyway.

He stopped driving through that part of town. He stopped going to the gas station chain where it happened. He stopped picking up the mail at the same time each day, because routine began to feel like a trap. His wife has learned not to touch him from behind without warning, but sometimes she forgets, and when she does, he flinches hard enough that she has started to cry. He apologizes. She says it is fine. It is not fine.

He has trouble sleeping. He lies awake in the dark and replays the moment in his head: the cold air, the voice asking for change, the flash of metal, the sound of his own teeth shattering. Sometimes the details shift. Sometimes the man is wearing a different jacket. Sometimes he sees the face of a student he used to counsel, the one whose father had a criminal record. He knows this is not real, but knowing does not stop the feeling. He has learned that the body remembers things the mind would rather forget.

The children at school know something is different. They do not say it, but the ones who have been through trauma themselves sometimes watch him with a quiet, knowing look. One girl, a senior, told him last week, “Mr. C., you seem kind of jumpy lately.” He laughed and said he was getting old. She did not smile. She knows what jumpy means.

He scored a 62 on the PCL-5 during an intake at a clinic his wife made him visit. He does not know what the number means, except that it is high. He does not ask. He goes to the sessions because she asked him to, and he has always done what she asked. But he does not talk about the parking lots, or the flinch, or the way he sometimes hears the sound of breaking bone when the school bell rings. He talks about the kids, about the weather, about how tired he is. He is always tired.

He is still in the office every morning at seven. He still wears the blazer. He still says the right things. But when he finishes his shift, he walks to his car with his keys between his fingers, and he does not relax until the locks click shut and he is alone.
